implementation_notes: The Android platform owns the component lifecycle: the system instantiates the activity and calls onCreate, onStart, onResume and their counterparts as the user navigates, and the process may be killed after onStop, so your code only fills in the hooks. Kotlin adds no structure of its own here - the inversion comes from overriding the platform's callback methods (or observing a Lifecycle in Compose) - and that is the right form whenever the component is managed by the platform. When the framework instead loads a module and invokes handlers, the coroutine form is lighter.
pitfalls: Callbacks arrive on the main thread and may run after the process was recreated; work started in onCreate must be cancelled in onDestroy or it outlives the instance.
Configuration changes recreate the activity, so state kept only in fields is lost between callbacks - saved state or a ViewModel is required.

variants.name: Engine-loaded modules and suspend handlers (Ktor)
variants.idiom_name: Ktor application modules and suspend route handlers
variants.implementation_notes: Ktor's engine owns the server: it loads each Application module function, invokes it to install plugins and routes, and then calls the matching route handler - a suspend function or lambda - for every request inside the application's coroutine scope. The framework base class is replaced by a module function plus handler lambdas, and suspension lets a handler await I/O without blocking an engine thread. Use explicit interface implementations when the extension contract must be shared across modules or checked at compile time.
pitfalls: Handlers run in the engine's coroutine scope: blocking calls (JDBC, Thread.sleep) stall an event-loop thread instead of suspending, so wrap them in withContext(Dispatchers.IO).
Anything captured by the module function lives as long as the application, so per-request state must stay inside the handler or the call object.
